ancient_source: Cao Cao's own claim in a letter to Sun Quan, quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary to Chen Shou's Sanguozhi (Wu Shu, vol. 47, biography of Sun Quan), citing Yu Pu's Jiangbiao Zhuan
modern_scholar: Rafe de Crespigny, following the contemporary counter-estimate attributed to Zhou Yu in the Sanguozhi
modern_citation: de Crespigny, R. (2010). Imperial Warlord: A Biography of Cao Cao, 155-220 AD. Leiden: Brill, pp. 183-184.
notes: Cao Cao's letter was a deliberate intimidation tactic and was doubted even by contemporaries; Zhou Yu's rebuttal (recorded in the same historiographic tradition) put the real figure near 220,000-240,000, including recently surrendered and unreliable former Jing-province troops. Classified as a personal ancient_claim rather than administrative_partisan since it is a general's own boast, not a later successor-dynasty compilation.

ancient_source: Tang-era Chinese accounts of the Abbasid army's size, as reported in modern secondary literature (Chang, 2023, p. 141); the specific primary text (Jiu Tangshu / Xin Tangshu / Zizhi Tongjian) could not be independently confirmed by direct inspection
modern_citation: Beckwith, C.I. (1993). The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia. Princeton University Press, p. 139, fn. 187.
notes: LOWER CONFIDENCE: the 200,000 figure for the Abbasid side is widely repeated in secondary literature as a Chinese-source claim, but I could not verify the exact primary-text locus (which Tang chronicle, which juan) against a live source, so this entry carries more locus uncertainty than the others in this set -- flagging per the project's verification standard rather than silently presenting it as fully nailed down. The Tang side's own claimed numbers (10,000-30,000 Tang plus Karluk allies) are much closer to Beckwith's modern estimate, so the inflation appears concentrated in Chinese reporting of the enemy's strength, consistent with a face-saving narrative for a Tang defeat.

ancient_source: Nihon Shoki: Saimei-tenno year 7 (661), 9th month (5,000 troops dispatched); Tenji-tenno year 2 (663), 3rd month (27,000 under Kamitsukeno no Kimi Wakako) and 8th month (10,000 under Iohara no Kimi). The commonly cited 42,000 total is a modern aggregation of these three separate entries
modern_citation: Noh Tae-don (2009). Samguk Tongil Jeonjaengsa [History of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms' Unification]. Seoul National University Press.
notes: The frequently cited 42,000 figure sums three separate Nihon Shoki dispatch entries spread over two years; it is not established that all three contingents were simultaneously present at Baekgang itself, and Noh Tae-don argues the scale of Yamato's commitment -- and the battle's supposed status as a decisive pan-East-Asian battle -- has been overstated in traditional narratives. The single 663/3 dispatch of 27,000 is the largest individually attested wave and is treated here as the better-supported deployed force. This is an own-side (Yamato) inflation of its own war effort rather than an enemy-directed exaggeration. Naval component (800 ships per Nihon Shoki) is not used here; this row is troops only, per the project's rule that ship counts are not troop counts.

ancient_source: Yuan Shi (official History of Yuan, compiled 1370 under the succeeding Ming dynasty), Riben zhuan (Japan biography): approx. 15,000 Mongol/Han Chinese/Jurchen troops plus 6,000-8,000 Korean troops and 7,000 Korean sailors
modern_citation: Conlan, T.D. (2001). In Little Need of Divine Intervention: Takezaki Suenaga's Scrolls of the Mongol Invasions of Japan. Ithaca: Cornell East Asia Series, p. 264.
notes: Conlan is a minority revisionist voice, not full scholarly consensus; from the logistics of the roughly 900-ship crossing and surviving Japanese muster/land documentation he argues neither side fielded more than a few thousand men. The Yuan Shi figure folds Korean sailors and logistics personnel into the headline troop count, matching this tradition's usual conflation of combatants and support personnel. Included as a citable, peer-reviewed estimate despite its minority status, per the rule against inventing a number rather than using an available real one.

ancient_source: Yuan Shi (official History of Yuan, compiled 1370 under the succeeding Ming dynasty), Riben zhuan (Japan biography): 40,000 from Korea aboard 900 ships plus 100,000 from southern China aboard 3,500 ships
modern_citation: Conlan, T.D. (2001). In Little Need of Divine Intervention: Takezaki Suenaga's Scrolls of the Mongol Invasions of Japan. Ithaca: Cornell East Asia Series, p. 264.
notes: Also labelled the Second Battle of Hakata Bay on Wikidata (Q2237622), spelled 'Kodan' there rather than the more usual romanization 'Koan'; verified live rather than assumed. Conlan questions whether even 10,000 Yuan soldiers actually landed and fought in Japan in 1281; this is a skeptical upper bound in his work rather than a precise point estimate, so the true figure could be lower still and this row likely understates the real log-ratio. The 100,000-strong southern-China contingent was drawn heavily from recently surrendered Southern Song troops together with associated logistics and labour personnel folded into the headline count, matching this tradition's pattern of conflating combatants and support staff. Minority revisionist position, included because it is a specific, citable estimate rather than an invented one.
